Course Description

The study of discrete mathematics provides an important foundation for basic theoretical principles in computer science. We first build a strong foundation in logic, formal proofs, and mathematical induction. We then examine the discrete structure of functions, relations, and graphs, which provide different ways of representing relationships, connections, and networks. Finally, we move onto numerical and computational aspects: number theory and modular arithmetic, counting and combinatorics, and discrete probability.

Learning Outcomes
  • Build a strong foundation for all of mathematics in proofs and logic.
  • Apply rigorous proof techniques, including direct proofs, proof by counterexample, proof by contradiction, and proof by induction.
  • Manipulate and describe relationships between sets of objects using relations and functions.
  • Understand basic concepts in graph theory and their usage in modeling a variety of computer science problems.
  • Understand basic concepts in number theory and their application to cryptography.
Pre-Requisites

High school level math

Materials

There are no required textbooks for this course. For optional additional reading, the recommended textbooks for this course are:

  • Scheinerman, Edward R. Mathematics: A Discrete Introduction(3rd edition, ISBN 9780840049421)
  • Kenneth H. Rosen,Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications(8th edition, ISBN 9781259731280)
There will not be any assignments or assigned readings from the text, but they are useful references for understanding the material.

Recitations

There is a required recitation section for this class on Fridays. Exact times are determined according to availability of students in the course. Recordings and practice problem solutions will be posted, and students will be expected to know the recitation material.

Grading

This course involves written homework assignments, two exams, and in-class assignments. Final grades are based on the instructor's holistic evaluation of your performance and follow Barnard's grading system. As a general guideline, assignments are weighted as follows:

  • Homework (30%): There will be weekly written homework assignments. Homework assignments must be typed. You may use use Word, LaTeX, or other text processing, but you may not submit a scan of a handwritten document. Solutions must be written individually. You may not use generative AI for your assignments.
  • Midterm (30%): The first exam will cover material from the first half of the course.
  • Final Exam (30%): The final exam is non-cumulative and will cover material from teh second half of the course.
  • Quizzes (10%): Throughout the semester we will have in-class quizzes. The quizzes are meant to be checks of understanding and will cover basic concepts from the lecture and/or previous lecture.

Course Policies

Collaboration

Students may discuss problems with one another and work toward solutions in small groups of their choosing (max 4 people). However, every student must individually write and submit solutions to the homework problems assigned themselves. The point of homework discussions is to help you understand the material. It is not acceptable to simply swap solutions, and every student should be able to orally explain every solution they submit. Looking at written homework solutions from the internet or other people is prohibited (this includes letting other students read your answers).

Generative AI Policy

The use of generative AI for assignments is prohibited in this class. You may use AI as a study tool to find practice problems or explain concepts, but you should not be using AI to solve homework assignments for you. It is also always forbidden to incorporate any substantive portion of an AI resource's output into your answers, even if you paraphrase it or rewrite it in your own words. If you think that the instructor might refuse to perform a certain task for you or answer a certain question during office hours, then you should definitely not be asking an AI resource to perform the same task or answer the same question.

Re-grade Requests

Any requests for regrades of assignments must be received within 2 weeks after the grade was received. If you request a regrade, we reserve the right to lower your grade if, upon re-review of your assignment, the original grading was found to be too generous. Any requests for regrades after this timeframe will not be considered.

Late Policy

Assignments may be submitted up to 5 days after the deadline for a penalty:

  • Less than 24 hours: 5% deduction
  • Between 1 and 2 days: 10% deduction
  • Between 2 and 3 days: 15% deduction
  • Between 3 and 4 days: 20% deduction
  • Between 4 and 5 days: 25% deduction
Assignments submitted 5 days or more after the deadline will receive no credit. The lowest homework assignment will be dropped.

Barnard Honor Code

You are expected to hold yourself to the highest standard of academic integrity and honesty, as reflected in the Barnard Honor Code. Approved by the student body in 1912 and updated in 2016, the Code states:

We, the students of Barnard College, resolve to uphold the honor of the College by engaging with integrity in all of our academic pursuits. We affirm that academic integrity is the honorable creation and presentation of our own work. We acknowledge that it is our responsibility to seek clarification of proper forms of collaboration and use of academic resources in all assignments or exams. We consider academic integrity to include the proper use and care for all print, electronic, or other academic resources. We will respect the rights of others to engage in pursuit of learning in order to uphold our commitment to honor. We pledge to do all that is in our power to create a spirit of honesty and honor for its own sake.

Affordable Access to Course Texts and Materials

All students deserve to be able to study and make use of course texts and materials regardless of cost. Barnard librarians have partnered with students, faculty, and staff to find ways to increase student access to textbooks. By the first day of advance registration for each term, faculty will have provided information about required texts for each course on CourseWorks (including ISBN or author, title, publisher, copyright date, and price), which can be viewed by students. A number of cost-free or low-cost methods for accessing some types of courses texts are detailed on the Barnard Library Textbook Affordability guide. Undergraduate students who identify as first- generation and/or low-income students may check out items from the FLI lending libraries in the Barnard Library and in Butler Library for an entire semester. Students may also consult with their professors, the Dean of Studies, and the Financial Aid Office about additional affordable alternatives for having access to course texts. Visit the guide and talk to your professors and your librarian for more details.
